question: Öömrang is a dialect of the North Frisian language spoken on the island of Amrum in the district of North Frisia. There are now trade mark registrations for terms and even whole sentences in the Frisian language and Öömrang. This development, understandably, is generating great uncertainty among the Frisian community concerned.

In principle, it is welcome that business operators recognise the marketing value of the regional specificities of North Frisia and its islands. However, Frisians are beginning to feel that their language is being sold out, something against which they are unable to defend themselves owing to the small size of their ethnic group.
The current legal situation discriminates against minority languages and the federal government and the EU as the politically responsible bodies must take action. 1.
What does the Commission intend to do together with the EUIPO to better protect the Frisian language, and is there a way to do this in an international context - e.g. together with the USA?
Should the EUIPO ensure that the provisions of the Charter of Fundamental Rights and the principles contained therein, in particular Articles 21 and 22, are respected when an EU trade mark is filed?

How can a provision be established under the EU Trade Mark Regulation – which bases the protection of any given term on the familiarity of the commercially relevant public with that term, which in the case of minority languages is naturally not great – to better ensure the protection of regional and minority languages by lowering this threshold?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.6.2024) Examination of EU trade mark (EUTM) applications is not limited to signs in EU official and working languages of the EU institutions1. Trade marks, which are devoid of any distinctive character, shall not be registered by the EU Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), as this constitutes one of the absolute grounds for refusal2.

This assessment is based on an objective test as defined by the Court of Justice of the European Union. Applications consisting of/containing Frisian words/expressions are examined like any other mark filed in a regional language.

When considering whether a language can be the basis for an objection, the Court of Justice ruled that the relevant test is to ask whether it is understood by a non-negligible part of the relevant public in at least part of the EU3. Therefore, the fact that a sign has a problematic meaning in an EU regional language can, under certain conditions, constitute a ground for refusal to register it.

All languages are treated equally and the fact that the language is not an EU official or working language is not a decisive criterion in EUIPO’s practice4. Furthermore, the EUIPO is tasked with the administration of the EUTM system established in the EUTM Regulation, which should be applied in a way that ensures full respect for fundamental rights and freedoms.

Even if ex officio checks of the EUIPO do not uncover an absolute ground for refusal to register, there are further safeguards to prevent or challenge registration. When EUTM applications are published, third parties may submit observations to the EUIPO when they consider that the sign in question should be refused on absolute grounds5.
After potential registration, it is possible to request cancellation of the registered trade mark6.
1 Within the meaning of Regulation No 1 determining the languages to be used by the European Economic

Community, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A01958R000120130701&qid=1716901390636 2 See Articles 7(1)(b) and 7(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/1001 on the European Union trade mark.

3 See Judgment of 6 October 2017, Ino Karelia v European Union Intellectual Property Office, T-878/16, EU:T:2017:702, paragraph 27; judgment of 25 November 2015, bd breyton-design GmbH v Office for Harmonisation in the Internal Market (Trade Marks and Designs), T-520/14, EU:T:2015:884, paragraph 29; judgment of 25 November 2015, Intesa Sanpaolo SpA v European Union Intellectual Property Office, T-529/15, EU:T:2016:747, paragraph 55.

4 Indeed, the EUIPO has refused marks because the ex officio check uncovered a meaning in the Frisian language for example, when it refused an application for the word mark Nij (EUTM 18 585 988, https://euipo.europa.eu/eSearch/#details/trademarks/018585988) or for the word mark Klötenköm (EUTM 1 616 814), decision confirmed by the Fifth Board of Appeal (Case R 1390/2022-5), https://euipo.europa.

eu/copla/trademark/data/W01616814/download/CLW/APL/2023/EN/20230405_R1390_202 2-5.doc?app=caselaw&casenum=R1390/2022-5&trTypeDoc=NA 5 Article 45 of Regulation (EU) 2017/1001. 6 See Article 63 of Regulation (EU) 2017/1001. Another safeguard after potential registration is provided by Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2017/1001.

This provision places an important limitation of the effects of an EU trade mark meaning that an EUTM proprietor cannot prohibit a third party from honestly using, in the course of trade signs which are not distinctive or which concern the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin, the time of production of goods or of rendering of the service, or other characteristics of the goods or services.
Bona fide traders operating in Frisian would be able to benefit from this provision.
